claims.text: The coupled tribo-corrosion response in high-entropy alloys is governed by cyclic disruption and rapid reformation of a multi-component passive oxide layer.
Mechanical wear locally removes the protective passive film.
Fresh metal exposed by film removal rapidly repassivates.
Rapid repassivation occurs because of the alloy's high configurational entropy.
The balance between oxide-removal and repassivation rates determines overall degradation and the relative mechanical and electrochemical contributions.
The initial alloy surface has a stable, multi-component passive oxide film formed under ambient, non-aggressive conditions.
Passive-film phase distribution and continuity modulate the alloy's resistance to degradation.
The high-entropy nature of the alloy may promote formation of a relatively robust reformed oxide layer.
Under tribo-corrosion, degradation will initially be accelerated relative to static corrosion or pure wear alone.
Tribo-corrosion will increase local corrosion at wear tracks.
Efficient repassivation will cause the degradation rate to moderate after an initial period and approach a quasi-steady state.
Static corrosion may exhibit consistently higher corrosion because wear-induced renewal of the oxide is absent.
Wear-only testing in a non-corrosive environment will produce primarily mechanical material loss.
Meaningful repassivation can occur when wear rate and corrosive aggressiveness are moderate.
Sufficiently severe wear can prevent repassivation.
Highly aggressive chemical conditions can prevent formation of a protective oxide layer.
Variations in alloy composition, environment, and wear parameters could change the predicted behavior.
Available evidence is insufficient to quantify oxide-removal and reformation kinetics under combined wear and corrosion.
A lack of significant non-additive degradation or a lack of demonstrable rapid oxide reformation would falsify the proposed governing mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis characterizes the intact passive film as protective and predicts increased local corrosion after wear disrupts it, but the outcome section also suggests that static corrosion without wear-induced film renewal may have consistently higher corrosion. The direction of the corrosion-component prediction relative to the static control is therefore internally inconsistent.

The falsification rule refers to a predicted synergistic, non-additive effect, whereas the predicted outcome only states that simultaneous exposure exceeds each single exposure and does not explicitly predict that total loss exceeds the sum of isolated wear and corrosion losses.
